hints: Think about what makes the d-block special, and remember the definition depends on the ion formed, not just the atom itself.
walkthrough:
Focus on the ion, not just the atom**
It is tempting to say any d-block metal, but that is not quite right. Think of scandium and zinc. Look at their stable ions, $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ is $3d^0$ and $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is $3d^{10}$. Neither has a partially filled d-subshell as an ion, so they are not transition elements.
Final answer: A transition element forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete / partially filled d-subshell.

hints: Recall the familiar colours of acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ before reduction, and the colours of their reduced products $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cr}^{3+}$.
walkthrough:
Link each oxidising agent to its reduction product**
Both $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ are being reduced by $\text{Sn}^{2+}$. In acid, $\text{MnO}_4^-$ goes to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ goes to $\text{Cr}^{3+}$. The $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ to $\text{Sn}^{4+}$ change is colourless to colourless, so it does not hide anything.

Remember the classic colour changes**
Dilute acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is intense purple and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ in dilute solution is very pale pink, often seen as colourless. Dilute acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ is orange and $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is green. With excess $\text{Sn}^{2+}$, reduction goes to completion, so you see the full change.

Final answer: For $\text{MnO}_4^-$: purple to pale pink / colourless ($\text{Mn}^{2+}$).
For $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$: orange to green ($\text{Cr}^{3+}$).

hints: Start from the two half-equations, $\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^-$ and $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and think how to cancel the electrons.
walkthrough:
Balance electrons between oxidation and reduction**
Tin is oxidised: $\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^-$. Chromium is reduced: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$. To cancel $6e^-$, you need three tin half-equations for every one dichromate half-equation.

Combine and check atoms and charge**
Adding gives $$3\text{Sn}^{2+} + \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 3\text{Sn}^{4+} + 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check Cr (2 to 2), O (7 to 7), H (14 to 14) and charge ($6 - 2 + 14 = +18$ on left, $12 + 6 = +18$ on right). State symbols $(aq)$ may be added.

hints: Think of coordination number as counting attachments to the central metal, each monodentate ligand donates one lone pair to form one coordinate bond.
walkthrough:
Count bonds to the metal**
Picture $\text{Ru}^{2+}$ in the middle with ligands all around it. Coordination number simply counts how many coordinate bonds are formed to that central ion. So coordination number six means six lone pairs are donated, giving six coordinate bonds to $\text{Ru}^{2+}$.
Final answer: Six coordinate / dative bonds / lone pairs donated to the central metal ion.

hints: Use coordination number six to work out how many $\text{NH}_3$ ligands must be present alongside one $\text{Cl}^-$ and one $\text{SO}_2$, then add up the charges.
walkthrough:
Work out the ligand set then the charge**
Coordination number is six and all ligands here are monodentate. You already have one $\text{Cl}^-$ and one $\text{SO}_2$, so the rest must be $6 - 1 - 1 = 4$ $\text{NH}_3$ molecules. Now add charges: $\text{Ru}^{2+} + \text{Cl}^- + 4(0) + 0 = +1$ overall. So the ion is $[\text{Ru}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}(\text{SO}_2)]^+$.

hints: Sketch an octahedron around Ru with four $\text{NH}_3$, one Cl and one $\text{SO}_2$ bonded through S, remembering to show the S atom directly attached to Ru.
Recall how to show 3D shape on paper using solid wedges for bonds coming out, hashed wedges for bonds going back, and normal lines for bonds in the plane.
Think where Cl and $\text{SO}_2$ can sit relative to each other to give two different forms, adjacent at 90 degrees or opposite at 180 degrees.
walkthrough:
Set up the octahedral framework**
With coordination number six, the shape is octahedral. Place Ru in the centre and arrange six ligands around it. Crucially, draw the $\text{SO}_2$ with its S atom joined to Ru, as $\text{Ru-SO}_2$, not $\text{Ru-O}$. Label all four $\text{NH}_3$ groups clearly.

Use 3D bonds correctly**
A flat cross is not enough. Use a solid wedge for a bond projecting out toward you, a hashed wedge for a bond projecting back, and straight lines for the four in-plane bonds. This shows the true octahedral geometry.

Draw cis versus trans**
In one box put Cl and $\text{SO}_2$ next to each other at $90^{\circ}$, this is the cis form. In the other box put Cl and $\text{SO}_2$ directly opposite each other at $180^{\circ}$, this is the trans form. The $\text{NH}_3$ ligands fill the remaining four positions in each case.

Final answer: Octahedral Ru with $4 \times \text{NH}_3$, $1 \times \text{Cl}$, $1 \times \text{SO}_2$ bonded via S in both diagrams, drawn with correct 3D wedge / hashed bonds.
One isomer has Cl and $\text{SO}_2$ adjacent (cis, $90^{\circ}$ apart), the other has Cl and $\text{SO}_2$ opposite (trans, $180^{\circ}$ apart).

hints: Remember the name given when the same ligands can be arranged differently in space around an octahedral centre, with identical groups either next to each other or opposite.
walkthrough:
Name the spatial arrangement change**
You have not changed which ligands are present, only their positions in space, cis versus trans. That is the classic geometrical or cis-trans isomerism seen in square planar and octahedral complexes.
Final answer: cis-trans / geometrical isomerism

hints: Start by thinking what ligands do to the energies of the five d-orbitals that are all at the same energy in a free ion.
Consider what happens when white light shines on the complex and only certain wavelengths provide exactly the energy gap for an electron to jump.
Link the colour you actually see to the light that is not absorbed, and describe the electron movement between the split d-orbitals.
walkthrough:
Split the d-orbitals**
In a free $\text{Ru}^{2+}$ ion the five d-orbitals have the same energy. When ligands approach to form coordinate bonds, they repel d-electrons unequally, so the d-orbitals split into two sets of different energy. The size of this gap depends on the metal, oxidation state and ligands.

Absorb light to promote an electron**
White light contains all visible wavelengths. If the energy of a photon exactly matches the gap between the lower and higher d-orbital sets, it is absorbed and an electron is excited or promoted from the lower set to the higher set. This is a d-d transition.

See the complementary colour**
Because certain wavelengths are removed by absorption, the light that passes through or is reflected is missing those colours. What you observe is the complementary colour of the light absorbed, which is why transition metal complexes are coloured.

Final answer: Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two sets of different energy.
Electrons absorb visible light and are promoted / excited to the higher energy d-orbital set.
The colour observed is the complementary colour to that absorbed.
